nodes.title: all 53 priceable campaigns priced the hedge at tailMs=0, so the gate admitted all 53
nodes.body:
e73 replays secondCandidateGate over every campaign's rounds, with the old tail estimator kept inline so the comparison is a replay and not a memory.

Result: 53 of 72 campaigns are priceable (they have at least one round with two sampled candidates and a measured wall clock).
- before the fix: 53 admitted, 0 refused
- after the fix: 42 admitted, 11 refused
- campaigns priced at exactly tailMs = 0 before: 53 of 53
- decisions flipped admit -> refuse: 11, refuse -> admit: 0, unchanged: 42
- tail after fix: min 15 ms, p50 531 ms, max 412,577 ms

The 11 flipped campaigns and their real tails: loom-acc1 (p=0.200, 165,775 ms), loom-acc2 (p=0.083, 50,692), loom-claim-live (p=0.250, 27,757), loom-demo-plan (p=0.200, 108,772), loom-probe (p=0.500, 300,367), loom-tri4 (p=0.800, 239,903), loom-tri7 (p=0.750, 160,867), loom-tri9 (p=0.667, 356,084), loom-ui3 (p=0.750, 275,794), loom-ui4 (p=0.750, 412,577), loom-ui5 (p=0.750, 242,469).

Only 11 flip because 42 have tails small enough that p(1-p)*roundMs still dominates. That is the honest number: the bug made the gate unconditional in the sense that refusal was unreachable, and the fix makes refusal reachable on 21% of the record.

nodes.title: a formula that is correct and a price that is not: the inputs are where the decisions actually live
nodes.body:
admitSecondCandidate computes EV = p(1-p)*roundMs - tailMs - marginMs from a single expression and its test suite covers the arithmetic thoroughly: p outside (0,1), negative margin, missing duration, exact break-even. All of those tests pass, and none of them could see the bug, because the bug is not in the function.

secondCandidateGate estimates tailMs as `slowest - sorted[floor(n/2)]`. With n = 2, sorted[floor(2/2)] = sorted[1] = the slowest attempt, so the estimate is `slowest - slowest = 0` for every two-candidate round. And two candidates is the only population the gate ever looks at, because `attempts.length >= 2` is its filter. So the price handed to the correct formula was identically zero on 100% of the input, EV was always positive, and the gate could only say yes.

This is the same shape as exp-cand-001 (found earlier by a probe that fed hand-built numbers), exp-gate-001 (minGain acting on binary scores), and exp-graded-003 (earned blocked by a boolean): the decision layer is fine, the measurement layer is degenerate. The general repair is not another rule about the decision; it is a cheap invariant on the input -- here, "a two-candidate round must price a non-zero tail unless both attempts took exactly the same time".

What made this instance findable was replaying the estimator over the whole record and printing the distribution of a single intermediate value (`tailMs`) rather than the final verdict. The verdict said "admit" 53 times, which looks like a working gate; the intermediate said "0" 53 times, which is obviously broken. Reporting one number per stage is what turns a plausible output into a legible one.

gaps.title: does the corrected gate change what a round buys, or is autoCandidateMode the only thing that ever decides?
gaps.body:
secondCandidateGate returns a price, but whether a round consults it depends on config.loopPolicy.autoCandidateMode and on an explicit secondCandidate. The record shows candidates: 2 in most rounds, which means the gate's answer was not the binding constraint in practice. So the 11 flipped decisions are a measurement of what the gate would have said, not of what the loop did.

What would decide it: whether any round in the record has candidateModeSource = 'record'. If none does, the estimator is tested but unwired, which is the same failure the second-candidate-gate test file was written to prevent ('a priced decision that no round consults is a comment with a test attached').
